answer.rationale: Only one lever can plausibly deliver an 18% spend cut this cycle: moving volume to the low-cost vendor. memory_c4 (renegotiate at renewal) is foreclosed by a stated current fact — the incumbent has refused to reopen price — so the negotiation path is dead on arrival regardless of how well it worked on day 29. memory_c1/c6 (renew, commit longer) protect delivery and integration but concede the cost mandate outright. memory_c5 (defer) is actively dangerous here: the contract does not auto-renew and the line is at 94% of committed volume with no buffer, so letting it lapse past the 14-day window converts a budget problem into a stoppage. That leaves memory_c2 as the single load-bearing memory, which is exactly why it is the one I spend the verification budget on. It is the thinnest of the set: it describes a shift made 'last year,' consolidated on day 38 from an archived record, and its supporting evidence is onboarding speed and invoicing accuracy — administrative signals, not sustained-delivery signals at high utilization. Accurate invoices tell me nothing about whether that vendor holds allocation when I am running with no slack. I want the original record to see the volume served, the duration observed, and whether any delivery misses were recorded, because the memory as consolidated may have compressed away precisely the failure modes that matter now. Hence the scale: a guarded partial shift with the incumbent kept as a bridge on short terms, not a wholesale cutover 14 days before expiry. This captures a real slice of the savings, generates first-party delivery data on the new vendor at current volumes, and keeps the single-point-of-failure lesson from memory_c3 in view — a full switch would simply relocate the dependency rather than remove it. The downstream risk I am explicitly flagging: if memory_c2's cost advantage was measured at lower volume or has since eroded, a broad rollout would lock in both a delivery gap and a cost figure that no longer exists, and future sessions would inherit that as settled fact. A guarded test keeps that correctable.
